\section[los nervios]{los nervios — nerves}

\label{lesson:ES-C710-nervios}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for nostalgia, then the Spanish for to long for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: los nervios}
\textbf{los nervios} — \textquotedblleft{}nerves\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Antes del examen tengo nervios.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I get nervous before the exam.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Tener nervios} — to be nervous. \emph{¡Qué nervios!} — I am so nervous!

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nervios} is the plural of \emph{nervio}, which comes from Latin \emph{nervus} \textquotedblleft{}sinew\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); the sense nerve came later, as in English \emph{nerve}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{los nervios}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{los nervios}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for nostalgia, then the Spanish for to long for, then say \emph{los nervios} again

\section[el estrés]{el estrés — stress}

\label{lesson:ES-C710-estres}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to long for, then the Spanish for nerves.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el estrés}
\textbf{el estrés} — \textquotedblleft{}stress\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El trabajo me causa estrés.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Work causes me stress.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Estar estresado} — to be stressed. Spanish adds an \emph{e-} before \emph{s} + consonant.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{estrés} was borrowed from English \emph{stress}, usually dated to the twentieth century; Spanish put an \emph{e-} in front, as it does with \emph{esnob} and \emph{escáner}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la ansiedad]{la ansiedad — anxiety}

\label{lesson:ES-C710-ansiedad}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for nerves, then the Spanish for stress.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la ansiedad}
\textbf{la ansiedad} — \textquotedblleft{}anxiety\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La ansiedad no me deja dormir.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Anxiety does not let me sleep.}
\end{quote}

Also eagerness: \emph{esperar con ansiedad}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ansiedad} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{anxietās} \textquotedblleft{}anxiety\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{anxius} \textquotedblleft{}troubled\textquotedblright{}; English \emph{anxious} comes from the same Latin.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la tensión]{la tensión — tension; blood pressure}

\label{lesson:ES-C710-tension}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for stress, then the Spanish for anxiety.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la tensión}
\textbf{la tensión} — \textquotedblleft{}tension; blood pressure\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Había mucha tensión en la reunión.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There was a lot of tension in the meeting.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Tomar la tensión} — to take someone's blood pressure (Spain); in Latin America \emph{la presión}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tensión} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{tēnsiō} \textquotedblleft{}a stretching\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{tendere} \textquotedblleft{}to stretch\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[calmar]{calmar — to calm, to soothe}

\label{lesson:ES-C710-calmar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for anxiety, then the Spanish for tension.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: calmar}
\textbf{calmar} — \textquotedblleft{}to calm, to soothe\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Esta música me calma.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{This music calms me.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Calmarse} — to calm down. \emph{¡Cálmate!} — Calm down!

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{calmar} is built on \emph{calma}, which comes from Late Latin \emph{cauma}, from Greek \emph{kauma} \textquotedblleft{}burning heat\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); at sea the hottest hours were the windless ones.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
